title: Chapter 4 — The Counterpane
paragraphs: Waking the next morning around daylight, I found Queequeg's arm thrown over me in the most loving and affectionate manner. You would almost have thought I was his wife. The counterpane was patchwork, full of odd little multicolored squares and triangles; and this arm of his, tattooed all over with an endless Cretan labyrinth of a figure, no two parts of which were exactly the same shade — owing, I suppose, to his keeping his arm at sea unmethodically in sun and shade, his shirtsleeves rolled up irregularly at various times — this same arm of his, I say, looked for all the world like a strip of that same patchwork quilt. Indeed, with the arm lying partly on it as it was when I first woke, I could hardly tell it from the quilt, they blended their colors together so; and it was only by the sense of weight and pressure that I could tell that Queequeg was hugging me.

My sensations were strange. Let me try to explain them. When I was a child, I well remember, something somewhat similar happened to me — whether it was real or a dream, I could never entirely settle. It was this. I had been up to some mischief or other — I think it was trying to crawl up the chimney, as I had seen a little chimney sweep do a few days before; and my stepmother, who somehow or other was always whipping me or sending me to bed without supper — my mother dragged me by the legs out of the chimney and packed me off to bed, though it was only two o'clock in the afternoon of the 21st of June, the longest day of the year in our hemisphere. I felt dreadful. But there was no help for it, so upstairs I went to my little room on the third floor, undressed as slowly as possible to kill time, and with a bitter sigh got between the sheets.

I lay there dismally calculating that sixteen entire hours must pass before I could hope for a resurrection. Sixteen hours in bed! The small of my back ached to think of it. And it was so light, too — the sun shining in at the window, a great rattling of coaches in the streets, and the sound of cheerful voices all over the house. I felt worse and worse. At last I got up, dressed, and, going softly downstairs in my stocking feet, sought out my stepmother and suddenly threw myself at her feet, begging her as a particular favor to give me a good slippering for my misbehavior — anything, indeed, but condemning me to lie in bed for such an unendurable length of time. But she was the best and most conscientious of stepmothers, and back I had to go to my room. For several hours I lay there wide awake, feeling a great deal worse than I have ever felt since, even from the greatest later misfortunes. At last I must have fallen into a troubled nightmare of a doze; and slowly waking from it — half steeped in dreams — I opened my eyes, and the room that had been sunlit was now wrapped in outer darkness. Instantly I felt a shock run through my whole frame; nothing was to be seen, and nothing was to be heard; but a supernatural hand seemed placed in mine. My arm hung over the counterpane, and the nameless, unimaginable, silent form or phantom to which the hand belonged seemed to be sitting close by my bedside. For what seemed ages piled on ages, I lay there, frozen with the most awful fears, not daring to drag my hand away, yet always thinking that if I could only stir it one single inch, the horrid spell would be broken. I don't know how this awareness at last slipped away from me; but waking in the morning, I shudderingly remembered it all, and for days and weeks and months afterward I lost myself in bewildering attempts to explain the mystery. Indeed, to this very hour, I often puzzle over it.

Now, take away the awful fear, and my sensations at feeling the supernatural hand in mine were very similar, in their strangeness, to those I experienced on waking up and seeing Queequeg's pagan arm thrown around me. But at length all the events of the past night soberly came back, one by one, in fixed reality, and then I was alive only to the comical predicament. For though I tried to move his arm — to unlock his bridegroom clasp — yet, sleeping as he was, he still hugged me tightly, as though nothing but death should part us two. I now tried to rouse him — "Queequeg!" — but his only answer was a snore. I then rolled over, my neck feeling as if it were in a horse collar, and suddenly felt a slight scratch. Throwing aside the counterpane, there lay the tomahawk sleeping by the savage's side, as if it were a hatchet-faced baby. A pretty pickle, truly, I thought; in bed here in a strange house in broad daylight, with a cannibal and a tomahawk! "Queequeg! In the name of goodness, Queequeg, wake up!" At length, by dint of much wriggling, and loud and incessant protests about the unseemliness of his hugging a fellow male in that matrimonial sort of style, I succeeded in extracting a grunt; and presently he drew back his arm, shook himself all over like a Newfoundland dog just out of the water, and sat up in bed, stiff as a pikestaff, looking at me and rubbing his eyes as if he did not altogether remember how I came to be there, though a dim awareness of knowing something about me seemed slowly to be dawning over him. Meanwhile, I lay quietly eyeing him, having no serious misgivings now, and intent on closely observing so curious a creature. When at last his mind seemed made up about the character of his bedfellow, and he had become, as it were, reconciled to the fact, he jumped out onto the floor, and by certain signs and sounds gave me to understand that, if I liked, he would dress first and then leave me to dress afterward, leaving the whole room to myself. Queequeg, I thought, under the circumstances this is a very civilized overture; but the truth is, these savages have an innate sense of delicacy, say what you will; it is marvelous how essentially polite they are. I pay this particular compliment to Queequeg because he treated me with so much civility and consideration, while I was guilty of great rudeness — staring at him from the bed and watching all his dressing motions, my curiosity for the time getting the better of my upbringing. Still, a man like Queequeg you don't see every day; he and his ways were well worth unusual attention.

He began dressing at the top by putting on his beaver hat — a very tall one, by the way — and then, still without his trousers, he hunted up his boots. What under heaven he did it for, I can't tell, but his next move was to crush himself — boots in hand and hat on — under the bed; and from various violent gaspings and strainings, I inferred he was hard at work booting himself, though by no law of propriety that I ever heard of is any man required to be private when putting on his boots. But Queequeg, you see, was a creature in the transition stage — neither caterpillar nor butterfly. He was just civilized enough to show off his outlandishness in the strangest possible ways. His education was not yet complete. He was an undergraduate. If he had not been a little civilized, he very probably would not have bothered himself with boots at all; but then, if he had not still been a savage, he would never have dreamed of getting under the bed to put them on. At last he emerged with his hat badly dented and crushed down over his eyes, and began creaking and limping about the room, as if, not being much used to boots, his pair of damp, wrinkled cowhide ones — probably not made to order, either — rather pinched and tormented him at the start of a bitter cold morning.

Seeing now that there were no curtains on the window, and that, the street being very narrow, the house opposite had a plain view into the room, and noticing more and more what an indecent figure Queequeg made, stomping about with little else on but his hat and boots, I begged him as well as I could to hurry his dressing somewhat, and especially to get into his trousers as soon as possible. He complied, and then proceeded to wash himself. At that time in the morning any Christian would have washed his face; but Queequeg, to my amazement, was content to restrict his washing to his chest, arms, and hands. He then put on his waistcoat, and, picking up a piece of hard soap from the washstand center table, dipped it in water and began lathering his face. I was watching to see where he kept his razor, when lo and behold, he takes the harpoon from the bed corner, slips off the long wooden shaft, unsheathes the head, whets it a little on his boot, and, striding up to the bit of mirror against the wall, begins a vigorous scraping — or rather harpooning — of his cheeks. Queequeg, I thought, this is using Rogers's best cutlery with a vengeance. Afterward I wondered less at this operation, when I came to know what fine steel the head of a harpoon is made of, and how extremely sharp its long straight edges are always kept.
The rest of his grooming was quickly finished, and he marched proudly out of the room wrapped in his great pilot monkey jacket, carrying his harpoon like a marshal's baton.
